title: Antão Gonçalves brings the first captives from West Africa to Portugal
place: Rio do Ouro, West African coast, and Portugal
summary: In 1441 Prince Henry sent the young captain Antão Gonçalves to the West African coast for seal skins and oil; Gonçalves resolved to take captives as well and, with Nuno Tristão, carried the first captives from the Rio do Ouro region back to Portugal.
account: The royal chronicler Gomes Eanes de Zurara records that “in this year 1441” Prince Henry armed a little ship under Antão Gonçalves, his chamberlain and “a very young man”, to bring back a cargo of the skins and oil of “sea-wolves” (seals).

Having taken that cargo, Gonçalves called together the one and twenty men of his ship and said, in Zurara's account: “O How fair a thing it would be if we, who have come to this land for a cargo of such petty merchandise, were to meet with the good luck to bring the first captives before the face of our Prince.” He then went inland by night with nine men to find inhabitants to seize.

Wikipedia's summary of Zurara's chronicle says Gonçalves captured a man and a woman; joining with Nuno Tristão's crew, they captured ten more, among them a nobleman named Adahu. Gonçalves returned to Portugal and in 1442 sailed again with the nobleman, whom he exchanged for ten slaves, some gold dust and ostrich eggs.

summary: In 1444 six caravels of Lagos merchants under Lançarote de Freitas raided the Arguin coast and brought 235 captives to Lagos, where they were divided among the owners before Prince Henry.
account: Lagos merchants, sometimes called the 'Lagos Company', obtained a licence from Prince Henry and sent six ships under Lançarote de Freitas to the Arguin banks in the spring of 1444. In a few days they seized about 235 people on the islands of Nar and Tider and nearby, and by early August 1444 the fleet was back in Lagos.

Zurara, who was there, records that “the Moors of that capture were in number 235.” On “the 8th of the month of August”, the captives were set ashore in a field outside the town and divided into fifths: “some kept their heads low and their faces bathed in tears, looking one upon another; others stood groaning very dolorously … others struck their faces with the palms of their hands, throwing themselves at full length upon the ground.” Fathers were parted from sons and husbands from wives.

Prince Henry watched mounted on horseback, received forty-six as his fifth and, Zurara says, “reflected with great pleasure upon the salvation of those souls that before were lost.” Lançarote was knighted for the enterprise. Lagos's slave market is described as opening in 1444.

title: Pope Nicholas V's bulls Dum Diversas and Romanus Pontifex

summary: Pope Nicholas V's bull Dum Diversas (1452) authorised Afonso V of Portugal to subdue 'Saracens and pagans' and consign them to perpetual servitude; Romanus Pontifex (1455) confirmed Portugal's claims in Africa and its monopoly of trade there.

With Romanus Pontifex, issued by Nicholas in 1455, it gave the Portuguese what they saw as moral justification to acquire slaves along the African coast by force or trade.

title: The encomienda, and the New Laws that were revoked
summary: From 1503 the Spanish Crown granted conquistadors encomiendas, the labour of whole Indigenous communities; the New Laws of 20 November 1542 limited them, but the restriction was repealed in 1545 after the encomenderos resisted.
account: Governor Nicolás de Ovando set up the formal encomienda on Hispaniola. Natives were forced into hard labour and punished, even killed, if they resisted.

Following the protests of Bartolomé de las Casas and others, Charles V issued the New Laws on 20 November 1542 to limit the encomenderos' power; encomiendas were to end on the holder's death. The encomenderos resisted: in Peru Gonzalo Pizarro led a revolt, and the first viceroy, Blasco Núñez Vela, was killed in 1546. The laws, passed in 1542, were repealed in 1545. The encomienda was legally ended only in 1720.

summary: In 1528 the conquistador Hernando Alonso, a converso who had built the brigantines for the siege of Tenochtitlan, was burned at the stake in Mexico on charges of Judaizing; the Holy Office was established in New Spain on 4 November 1571, and on 8 December 1596 nine members of the Carvajal circle were burned.
account: Hernando Alonso, one of the shipbuilders who built the brigs for the siege of Tenochtitlan, was arrested in 1528 on charges of Judaizing, tortured until he confessed, and burned at the stake; he was the first person burned at the stake in the New World, and his brother Gonzalo de Morales was burned the same day. On 8 December 1596 most of the extended family of Luis de Carvajal y de la Cueva, including his sister Francisca and her children, nine people in all, were tortured and burned. A plaque at the convent of San Diego marks the quemadero, the burning place, used from 1596 to 1771.

title: The Pequot War and the Mystic massacre
place: Mystic River, Connecticut, and southern New England
summary: In 1636–1638 the English colonies of New England and their Narragansett and Mohegan allies destroyed the Pequot nation; at Mystic on May 26, 1637 colonists set the Pequot fort ablaze and killed between 400 and 700 people, and hundreds of captives were enslaved.
account: The Pequot War was fought from 1636 to 1638 between the Pequot nation and the Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth and Saybrook colonists with their Narragansett and Mohegan allies. On the night of May 26, 1637 a Connecticut force under Captain John Mason, joined by Captain John Underhill and allied Natives, surrounded the fortified Pequot village near the Mystic River; Mason ordered it set ablaze and its two exits blocked, and those who tried to escape over the palisade were shot or killed outside. Between 400 and 700 Pequots were killed. Underhill wrote that “there were about foure hundred soules in this Fort, and not above five of them escaped out of our hands.”

The Treaty of Hartford of 1638 forbade the Pequots to return to their lands, speak their language or call themselves Pequots, and the colonial authorities classed them as extinct; a western band kept its sovereignty and is today a federally recognized nation.

title: The Pueblo Revolt
place: Santa Fe de Nuevo México (New Mexico)
summary: On August 10, 1680 most of the Pueblo towns of New Mexico rose together against Spanish rule, killing 400 Spaniards including 21 of the 33 Franciscan missionaries and driving the remaining 2,000 settlers out of the province for twelve years.
account: From 1540 the Pueblo people suffered successive Spanish incursions, the persecution of their traditional religion, and massacres such as Ácoma in 1599. In 1675 Governor Juan Francisco Treviño arrested forty-seven medicine men for “sorcery”; three were hanged and the rest whipped. Among those released was Popé of Ohkay Owingeh, who spent five years organizing a revolt among the 46 Pueblo towns.

Popé sent runners to the towns carrying knotted cords, one knot to be untied each morning; when the last knot was untied they rose. On August 10, 1680 the Puebloans took the Spaniards’ horses, sealed the roads to Santa Fe and attacked the settlements. A total of 400 people were killed, including 21 of the 33 Franciscan missionaries in New Mexico, and the remaining 2,000 settlers fled the province. The Spaniards returned twelve years later.

title: The Supreme Court’s Indian cases: discovery, dependency and Worcester
place: Washington, D.C.; the Cherokee Nation, Georgia
summary: In three cases Chief Justice John Marshall’s court laid down the doctrine of discovery (1823), called the Cherokee a “domestic dependent nation” (1831), and upheld Cherokee sovereignty against Georgia (1832), a ruling that did not save them from removal.
account: In Johnson v. M’Intosh (1823) Marshall set out the “discovery doctrine”: a European power gains sovereignty over the land it discovers and the exclusive right to extinguish the Native occupants’ “right of occupancy”. In Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (March 18, 1831) he held that the Cherokee Nation was not a foreign nation but a “domestic dependent nation”, its relation to the United States like that of “a ward to its guardian”.

In Worcester v. Georgia (March 3, 1832) the Court struck down Georgia’s law barring non-Natives from Cherokee land without a state license, building the foundations of tribal sovereignty. Jackson wrote that the decision “has fell still born”; the words “John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it!” are believed to be apocryphal. On December 29, 1835 a few Cherokees without authority signed the removal Treaty of New Echota; Justice Stephen Breyer later observed that the Cherokee nation was the “obvious loser”.

title: The Black Codes
place: Mississippi, South Carolina and the other former Confederate states
summary: In 1865 and 1866 the legislatures of the former slave states passed Black Codes: laws that limited the freedom of the newly emancipated and forced them back into labor for white employers.

The codes granted some limited rights, such as owning personal property and marrying, but black people were barred from testifying against white people and faced severe penalties for unemployment. Intense Northern reaction against the Mississippi and South Carolina laws led some later states to remove overt racial language, while keeping vagrancy and apprenticeship laws that worked to the same end.

title: Convict leasing

date.text: Expanded after 1865; peaked about 1880; phased out after December 12, 1941

summary: Using the Thirteenth Amendment's exception for punishment of crime, Southern states leased prisoners, the great majority of them Black men convicted under the Black Codes and vagrancy laws, to planters and companies.
account: Louisiana leased out convicted people as early as 1844, and the system expanded throughout most of the South with emancipation in 1865. Its constitutional basis was the 1865 Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished slavery and involuntary servitude “except as a punishment for crime”.

Black Codes, pig laws and vagrancy laws criminalized unemployment, homelessness and changes of employment, creating a new criminal class of freed people. By the 1880s Black people made up 80 to 90 percent of those incarcerated in the South.

The system was highly lucrative: in 1898, 73 percent of Alabama's annual state revenue came from convict leasing. title: Forty acres taken back and the Freedman's Bank fails

place: Sea Islands and coast of Georgia and South Carolina; Washington, D.C.
summary: Sherman's Special Field Orders No. 15 set aside land in plots of up to 40 acres for freed families, but President Andrew Johnson reversed the policy in 1865; the Freedman's Savings Bank, chartered the same year, failed in 1874 with the savings of its depositors.
account: On January 16, 1865, General William T. The Freedman's Savings and Trust Company was chartered by Congress on March 3, 1865, to collect deposits from Black people, especially the formerly enslaved. title: Sharecropping and the crop lien

date.text: Widespread from Reconstruction (1865–1877); declined from the late 1930s and 1940s

summary: After the Civil War most freed people, with no land, worked white-owned land for a share of the crop, bound by debt to the landowner or merchant.
account: Under sharecropping, landowners provided land, housing, tools and seed, and merchants supplied food on credit; at the end of the season the cropper paid the owner a share of the crop, typically one-half to two-thirds. If what was left came to less than what he owed, he remained in debt. Under the crop lien the planter or merchant took the year's crop as collateral and settled the debt when it was sold.

Sharecropping became widespread in the South during Reconstruction (1865–1877), after President Johnson returned the land set aside by Sherman's Field Order No. 15. In Mississippi by 1900, 85 percent of black farmers were tenants or sharecroppers. Around Elaine, Arkansas, landowners kept sharecroppers in debt through plantation-store prices and underpayment for crops, and it was an unwritten law that a sharecropper could not leave until his debts were paid.
Traditional sharecropping declined after farm mechanization became economical in the late 1930s and early 1940s, and many sharecroppers moved to the cities.

account: The Birth of a Nation is a 1915 silent film directed by D. W. Griffith, released on February 8, 1915, and based on Thomas Dixon Jr.'s 1905 novel and play The Clansman. It was screened inside the White House and watched by President Woodrow Wilson.

The Ku Klux Klan is portrayed as a heroic force that protects white women and maintains white supremacy. Black leaders and the NAACP campaigned unsuccessfully to have it banned as inflaming racial tensions, and it has been acknowledged as an inspiration for the rebirth of the Klan a few months after its release.

title: Harlem's Hebrew congregations: Matthew, Herman and Ford

date.text: 1919 (Commandment Keepers), 1921 (Moorish Zionist Temple), 1930 (Ford to Ethiopia), 1935 (Ford's death)

summary: In Harlem between 1919 and 1931 at least eight Black Hebrew congregations were founded, among them Wentworth Arthur Matthew's Commandment Keepers (1919), Mordecai Herman's Moorish Zionist Temple (1921) and Arnold Josiah Ford's Beth B'nai Israel; in 1930 Ford led a group to Ethiopia.
account: In Harlem alone at least eight Black Hebrew groups were founded between 1919 and 1931. Wentworth Arthur Matthew (1892–1973), an immigrant from Saint Kitts (he sometimes said Lagos), founded the Commandment Keepers of the Living God in Harlem in 1919. Influenced by Marcus Garvey's pan-Africanism, he developed it along Jewish lines of observance; it was originally a Christian church and increasingly de-emphasized Jesus Christ. He incorporated it in 1930 and founded a rabbinical academy in Brooklyn. He was twice refused membership of the New York Board of Rabbis.

Mordecai Herman, a West Indian immigrant and a member of Garvey's UNIA, founded the Moorish Zionist Temple at 127 West 134th Street in Harlem in 1921, blending the belief that Black people descend from the Israelites with aspects of traditional Judaism, Christianity and pan-African nationalism.

Arnold Josiah Ford (1877–1935), born in Barbados, directed the UNIA's band and choir and co-wrote its Universal Ethiopian Anthem. After Garvey's conviction he founded Beth B'nai Israel in a Harlem storefront. In 1930 he and a small group of Black Jews went to Ethiopia, took part in Haile Selassie's coronation and acquired 800 acres of land; he died there in 1935. Matthew had been his student.

summary: In the Red Summer of 1919 white supremacist terror and race riots struck more than three dozen U.S. cities; the deadliest violence fell on black sharecroppers organizing around Elaine, Arkansas.
account: The Red Summer was a period in mid-1919 of white supremacist terrorism and race riots in more than three dozen cities and one rural county in Arkansas; the name was coined by James Weldon Johnson of the NAACP. Many African Americans fought back, notably in Chicago and Washington, D.C.

From September 30 to October 2, 1919, around Elaine in Phillips County, Arkansas, where black sharecroppers were organizing against peonage, white mobs aided by federal troops killed an estimated 100 to 240 black people; five white men were killed. State officials claimed a black insurrection; more than 100 African Americans were indicted and 12 sentenced to death.

title: The Jones Act binds Puerto Rico's shipping
summary: The Merchant Marine Act of 1920, whose Section 27 is the Jones Act, requires goods shipped between U.S. ports, including Puerto Rico, to travel on U.S.-built, U.S.-owned and U.S.-crewed ships.
account: The Merchant Marine Act of 1920 was introduced by Senator Wesley Jones and signed by President Woodrow Wilson on June 5, 1920. Its Section 27, the Jones Act, deals with cabotage: all goods carried by water between U.S. ports must travel on ships built in the United States, flying the U.S. flag, owned by U.S. citizens and crewed by U.S. citizens and permanent residents.

The act prevents foreign-flagged ships from carrying cargo between the contiguous United States and Puerto Rico, Hawaii, Alaska and Guam. Critics say it more than doubles shipping costs to Puerto Rico; a 2013 government study found the exact effect on freight rates hard to isolate.

title: Virginia's Racial Integrity Act
summary: Virginia's Racial Integrity Act of 1924 required birth and marriage certificates to record every person as 'white' or 'colored', classifying Native Americans as colored.
account: In 1924 the Virginia General Assembly enacted the Racial Integrity Act, pushed by Walter Plecker, registrar of the Virginia Bureau of Vital Statistics. It required that all birth and marriage certificates in Virginia record the person's race as either "white" or "colored", and it classified all non-whites, including Native Americans, as colored.

It prohibited interracial marriage. A 1930 act defined anyone with even a trace of sub-Saharan African ancestry as black, codifying the so-called one-drop rule. Its proponents were spurred on by Native groups such as the Chickahominy and Rappahannock asserting their identities, and racialization became a tool for dispossession. The Supreme Court overturned the act in 1967 in Loving v. Virginia.

title: The Mexican Repatriation
place: United States, especially California and Texas
summary: During the Great Depression the United States deported and pressured into leaving hundreds of thousands of Mexicans and Mexican Americans, many of them U.S.-born citizens.
account: The Mexican Repatriation was the repatriation or deportation of Mexicans and Mexican Americans from the United States during the Great Depression, between 1929 and 1939. About 82,000 people were formally deported and others left under pressure; estimates of the number who moved to Mexico range from 300,000 to 2 million, most between 500,000 and 1 million.

An estimated forty to sixty percent of those repatriated were citizens of the United States, overwhelmingly American-born children. Some scholars tie the large number of deportations between 1929 and 1933 to the policy of the Hoover administration.

California apologized in 2005 through the Apology Act for the 1930s Mexican Repatriation Program, recognizing the unconstitutional removal and coerced emigration of U.S. citizens and legal residents of Mexican descent; Los Angeles County apologized in 2012.

summary: On August 7, 1930, a mob of thousands lynched Thomas Shipp and Abram Smith in Marion, Indiana; the photograph of their bodies inspired the poem and song “Strange Fruit.”

Police officers in the crowd cooperated. A third prisoner, 16-year-old James Cameron, narrowly escaped.

A local photographer, Lawrence Beitler, photographed the bodies surrounded by a crowd estimated at 5,000, including women and children, and sold thousands of copies in ten days. Abel Meeropol cited the photograph as the inspiration for his poem, published as “Bitter Fruit” in January 1937 in a teachers' union magazine; Billie Holiday recorded “Strange Fruit” in 1939.
The Tuskegee Institute recorded the lynchings of 3,446 Blacks and 1,297 Whites between 1882 and 1968, with the peak in the 1890s; lynchings declined considerably by the Great Depression.

title: The Rhoads letter in Puerto Rico
summary: In November 1931 Rockefeller Institute pathologist Cornelius Rhoads wrote a letter from Puerto Rico calling Puerto Ricans a degenerate race and claiming he had killed eight and transplanted cancer into others; Pedro Albizu Campos made it public in 1932.
account: In 1931 Cornelius P. Rhoads joined the Rockefeller Anemia Commission at Presbyterian Hospital in San Juan, where the group had more than 200 patients, primarily clinical subjects. On November 10, 1931, he wrote an unmailed letter calling Puerto Ricans “the dirtiest, laziest, most degenerate and thievish race of men ever inhabiting this sphere” and claiming he had furthered their extermination by killing eight and transplanting cancer into several more.

In early 1932 a lab assistant gave the letter to the nationalist leader Pedro Albizu Campos, who publicized it and charged that Rhoads was part of a U.S. plot to exterminate Puerto Ricans. An investigation by the Puerto Rican Attorney General reviewed the files of 257 patients, including 13 who died, and found no evidence of the crimes described; Rhoads called his words a joke.

Rhoads went on to lead Memorial Hospital and Sloan-Kettering and appeared on the cover of Time in 1949. In 2002 an investigation led by Jay Katz for the American Association for Cancer Research found no evidence of unethical human experimentation but judged the letter so offensive that the association removed Rhoads's name from its award.

title: The Tuskegee syphilis study begins
summary: In 1932 the U.S. Public Health Service began a study of untreated syphilis in 600 Black men in Macon County, Alabama, deceiving them and withholding treatment for forty years.
account: In 1932 the U.S. Public Health Service, working with the Tuskegee Institute, began a study to record the natural history of syphilis, the “Tuskegee Study of Untreated Syphilis in the Negro Male.” It enrolled 600 impoverished Black sharecroppers, 399 with latent syphilis and 201 without. Their informed consent was not collected; they were told they were being treated for “bad blood” and promised free medical care.

The men were told the study would last six months; it lasted forty years. By 1943 penicillin was the treatment of choice, and by 1947 it was standard, but the men were not offered it, and researchers kept them from treatment elsewhere.

The study ended in 1972 after an Associated Press story. By then 28 of the men had died of syphilis and 100 of related complications, 40 of their wives had been infected, and 19 of their children had been born with congenital syphilis. President Bill Clinton apologized on May 16, 1997.

title: Termination and relocation

Public Law 280 the same year let states take jurisdiction over reservations. Between 1953 and 1964 more than 100 tribes and bands were terminated, affecting more than 12,000 Native people, 3% of the Native population.

The Indian Relocation Act, signed by Eisenhower on August 3, 1956, offered vocational training to draw Native people off the reservations into the cities; it has been characterized as part of the termination policy, weakening community and tribal ties. In 1950 only 6% of American Indians lived in urban areas; by 1960 more than 31,000 had moved to cities since 1952, about 30% of them returning, and some found poverty, joblessness and homelessness there instead of the promised help.

title: Brown v. Board of Education
summary: On May 17, 1954 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously that state-sanctioned segregation of public schools violated the 14th Amendment, overturning the 'separate but equal' rule of Plessy v. Ferguson (1896).
account: Chief Justice Earl Warren delivered the unanimous ruling in Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, Kansas, on May 17, 1954. summary: From April 2016 thousands joined the Standing Rock Sioux to stop the Dakota Access Pipeline under Lake Oahe, near their water source and sacred sites; protesters were met with attack dogs, pepper spray and water cannon, and the camps were cleared in February 2017.

In April 2016 youth from Standing Rock began a campaign to stop it. On September 3, 2016 the company bulldozed ground the tribe had identified as containing possible burial sites; private security used attack dogs and pepper spray, and at least six protesters were treated for dog bites. A United Nations expert said the tribe had been excluded from consultation.

In November 2016 police used tear gas and water cannon on protesters in freezing weather. On December 4, 2016 the Army said it would not grant the easement under Lake Oahe, but in early 2017 the Army Corps of Engineers granted it. The last protesters were evicted by the National Guard and police on February 23, 2017.

title: The Southern Poverty Law Center lists Israel United in Christ as a hate group

date.text: First in the report published February 4, 2016 (for 2015); listed for 2015–2018, 2021 and 2022

summary: The Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) listed Israel United in Christ among active hate groups in its annual reports for 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2021 and 2022; IUIC denies it is a hate group.
account: The SPLC, a nonprofit legal advocacy organization in Montgomery, Alabama, has published an annual census of hate groups since 1990. Its report “Active Hate Groups in the United States in 2015,” published February 4, 2016, included Israel United in Christ among its black separatist and black nationalist groups, and IUIC appears in the SPLC’s lists for 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2021 and 2022. In 2008 the SPLC had written that “the extremist fringe of the Hebrew Israelite movement” had a Black supremacist outlook, while also writing that “most Hebrew Israelites are neither explicitly racist nor anti-Semitic and do not advocate violence.”

In 2019 Heidi Beirich of the SPLC told the BBC that the center lists IUIC as a “black nationalist hate group” and “racist”: “racist against white people, racist against Jews,” and “incredibly homophobic, as well.” The Oklahoman reported in 2022 that the SPLC designated IUIC a hate group “notably due to what the nonprofit law center described as the group’s anti-white, anti-Semitic and anti-LGBTQ messaging,” and placed it among groups espousing “Radical Hebrew Israelites” ideology.

IUIC denies that it is a hate group. It told the BBC that “at no point do we teach against the laws of the land or authorities.” Bishop Kani told The Oklahoman the group had been “mislabeled”: “We don’t promote violence, we’re not out there looking to harm people… they translate when we talk as hate because we’re trying to empower ourselves.” Many of IUIC’s videos open with the disclaimer “We are not a hate group,” and its website tells members to notify the authorities of any plot to cause harm or break the laws of the land.

points: Once a group is put on the hate list, it becomes a target: every IUIC branch is listed with its address and phone number, so that somebody will come in and do something. That is why the schools keep security.
teaching.quote: They're trying to stir people up against us.

title: The FBI’s “Black Identity Extremists” designation

date.text: Report dated August 3, 2017; designation used until July 2019

summary: From August 2017 to July 2019 the FBI used the designation “Black Identity Extremists,” first in a counterterrorism report dated August 3, 2017 sent to thousands of police departments; critics said it described a movement that did not exist.
account: “Black Identity Extremists” first appeared in an FBI counterterrorism report dated August 3, 2017 and sent to thousands of American police departments, describing safety concerns about allegedly violent African-American activists. Foreign Policy published the leaked report in October 2017; it stated that “[t]he FBI assesses it is very likely Black Identity Extremist perceptions of police brutality against African Americans spurred an increase in premeditated, retaliatory lethal violence against law enforcement.” Former government officials and legal experts said the term described a movement that did not exist.

In November 2017 the National Organization of Black Law Enforcement Executives called the designation “ill advised,” and in March 2018 it was discussed in the Congressional Black Caucus. Civil liberties groups warned it would treat Black activism as equivalent to white supremacist violence. The FBI dropped the term in July 2019, merging several categories under “racially motivated violent extremism”; according to the ACLU, leaked documents showed a program called IRON FIST continued to investigate Black activists.

points: Representative Karen Bass pressed the Attorney General on the report, Black Identity Extremists likely motivated to target law enforcement officers, and showed that the organizations it named were from decades ago and that no such group exists. When it was proved there was no Black identity extremist group, they set out to manufacture one: the Jersey City attack was made to serve that purpose.

title: The murder of Joy Morgan, and the charges laid against the church

date.text: Last seen December 26, 2018; conviction August 5, 2019; inquest 2021

summary: Joy Morgan, a 20-year-old midwifery student and member of IUIC’s UK branch, was murdered after a church celebration on December 26, 2018; fellow member Shohfah-El Israel was convicted on August 5, 2019, and coverage of the case carried her family’s and the SPLC’s charges against the church, which IUIC denied.
account: Joy Morgan, born February 12, 1998, was a midwifery student at the University of Hertfordshire. She joined the UK branch of Israel United in Christ in Ilford, east London, in January 2016, ran its children’s group, and two weeks before she went missing said in a video, “IUIC is my family and like the best family that I’ve ever had.” She was last seen alive on December 26, 2018 at a church celebration in Ilford. She was reported missing on February 7, 2019, after her housemates had not seen her since Christmas.

Police arrested fellow member Shohfah-El Israel (born Ajibola Shogbamimu) on February 9, 2019 on the M25; he was charged with murder on February 27. He admitted spending two nights alone with her at his Cricklewood flat, which broke the church’s rule against women being alone with men other than their husbands. A jury at Reading Crown Court convicted him on August 5, 2019, and he was sentenced to life with a minimum of 17 years; he refused to say where her body was. Her remains were found in woodland near Stevenage in October 2019. A 2021 coroner’s inquest could not establish how she died.

The coverage carried charges against the church. Her mother Carol said her daughter had been turned into a racist by the church and called it a cult, and her family said she had grown distant and called her mixed-race younger sister a “demon” and a “white devil.” Former members told the BBC of harsh discipline and of being told to cut off unbelieving family. The prosecutor described a strict hierarchy in which women had no rank. The SPLC described IUIC as a “hate group” and “a black nationalist group.”

IUIC denied these claims. It told the BBC that former members who speak against it are “disgruntled,” that claims it encourages members to cut off their families are “lies,” and that “at no point do we teach against the laws of the land or authorities.” The church described Shohfah-El Israel as an “enthusiastic” member and said he had once been demoted from the rank of soldier over his behaviour. Evidence given at the trial indicated that Joy Morgan had a good relationship with the church and its congregants, and police found no reliable indication that she wanted to leave it.

points: Years after her death, other camps print Joy Morgan’s picture and teach in the street that IUIC had something to do with her death, all the way over in England, while they say nothing of a 13-year-old girl abused by a man who called himself a Hebrew Israelite. All Israelite groups are not the same, and IUIC has no affiliation with those groups.
So the chief priests and Pharisees followed Christ’s camp and sought to lay hands on him, but feared the multitude: digging into a member’s personal life is to turn the multitude against us.

title: McGirt v. Oklahoma
summary: On July 9, 2020 the Supreme Court held that the reservation promised to the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in the 19th century was never disestablished and remains Indian country, so Oklahoma could not prosecute Native people for major crimes there.
account: Before statehood in 1907 about half of Oklahoma, including Tulsa, belonged to the Five Tribes: the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee Creek and Seminole. The case was brought by Jimcy McGirt, an enrolled member of the Seminole tribe. Writing for a 5–4 majority, Justice Gorsuch held that the Muscogee domain remains Indian country under the Major Crimes Act: “Because Congress has not said otherwise, we hold the government to its word.” He rejected the argument that “the price of keeping” the promises “has become too great.”

Oklahoma’s Court of Criminal Appeals applied McGirt to rule that nine other nations’ reservations had not been disestablished, but held it was not retroactive. In Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta (2022) the Supreme Court held that the state shares jurisdiction over crimes by non-Natives against Natives in Indian country.

title: IUIC opens its headquarters school, its first building
summary: IUIC opened a new headquarters school in New York, which its members built themselves; the grand opening was published in December 2015 and again in April 2016.
account: IUIC’s class channel published “The Israelites: IUIC HEADQUARTERS NEW SCHOOL GRAND OPENING” on 9 December 2015 and “IUIC HEADQUARTERS SCHOOL GRAND OPENING” on 13 April 2016.

points: Any leader who is not thinking forward about building and maintaining Israelite-owned institutions is not worth your time. Faith without works is dead, as James says: if a brother or sister is destitute of daily food, words alone profit nothing.
Those who give up everything and jeopard their lives are the ones who will judge the nations and have dominion over the people.
The little school was designed and wired by the brothers themselves, Deacon Yawasap among them, and built by the craftsmen of the congregation.

source.title: The Israelites: IUIC HEADQUARTERS NEW SCHOOL GRAND OPENING

points: The move from the old school, a little basement in the Bronx that the brothers fixed up, was a stepping stone. The new building had no walls, no electricity and no water, but the brothers had the trades and did it themselves, despite people saying it would never happen.

One member who came in 2006 recalled the road: an elder’s home in Coney Island, Brooklyn; then a basement on Long Island; then Brooklyn; then the Bronx; and now this building. You shall know them by their fruits.

source.title: IUIC HEADQUARTERS SCHOOL GRAND OPENING

points: IUIC has existed since 2003 and got its first building in 2015. That was many years from the beginning, but the vision stayed and nobody gave up; the second building followed.

source.title: #IUIC | PATIENT SAINTS RADIO: June 26, 2022

scriptures.why: Faith without works is dead: a leader must build institutions that meet the people’s needs.
Those who give everything for the work will judge the nations and have dominion over the people.

title: IUIC’s mission to Liberia
summary: In early 2018 an IUIC delegation travelled to Liberia to teach the remnant of Israel there; the class reported on the mission on 8 April 2018.

points: In Liberia the delegation met the same problems the apostles met with the first converts in Acts 15: some still worshipped other gods, there was fornication, people ate things strangled such as bush meat, and blood. That is why those four things were named.
The congregation there had been watching online, and IUIC will have to work very closely with them. The delegation will go back.

title: IUIC marches in Aruba and Curaçao
summary: In December 2023 IUIC members marched in Aruba and then in Willemstad, Curaçao, handing out pamphlets; the press reported the march as peaceful.
account: Curacao.nu reported on 15 December 2023 that members of IUIC, recognisable by their lilac shirts and black trousers, had marched on the island the day before, handing out pamphlets in the city centre and elsewhere. The march followed a similar action in Aruba and was peaceful; police and the Vrijwilligers Korps Curaçao were present and no disturbances were reported. The report called the visit a sign of IUIC’s growing influence beyond the United States.

points: The press itself recorded that the march was peaceful. IUIC is peaceful, and its work will prove it.
The report’s own words show the work growing: IUIC’s visit to the Caribbean islands demonstrates its expansion beyond the United States.
